children: Facing impending patent expirations on its key moneymakers, Bristol Myers Squibb notched a win in a cancer-therapy trial. But mixed results for another pipeline candidate threaten to temper the momentum.

Bristol Myers announced Monday that targeted cancer therapy RYZ101 significantly improved progression-free survival in a Phase 3 trial of patients with rare, advanced gastrointestinal and pancreatic tumors.

The trial tested RYZ101 against the standard of care in patients whose disease had progressed after Lutetium-177-based therapy, which uses isotopes to deliver localized radiation to cancer cells. Progression-free survival is a measure of how long a patient lives during and after treatment without their disease worsening.

While developing cancer drugs is notoriously complex, pharmaceutical companies continue to prioritize oncology as they channel resources into the search for more effective treatments. An IQVIA report found that oncology accounted for the largest share of trial starts in 2025, representing 38% of all Phase I to Phase III industry-sponsored trials.

Demand and market growth for new cancer therapies have accelerated substantially in recent years, reshaping the treatment landscape. One-third of trials last year involved novel therapeutic modalities including antibody-drug conjugates, radiopharmaceuticals, gene therapies, and multi-specific antibodies, marking a threefold increase over the past decade.

Radiopharmaceuticals, which are gaining momentum in both cancer diagnosis and treatment, have drawn increased attention following GE HealthCare's purchase of Sofie Biosciences last week. Bristol Myers officially entered the space in 2023 with its $4.1 billion acquisition of RayzeBio, the original developer of RYZ101.
However, Bristol Myers stock slid 2.9% on Monday, reversing direction from premarket trading. The decline appeared to be driven by trial results for a different pipeline candidate.

Also on Monday, Bristol Myers reported that a lower dose of its experimental drug admilparant met the main goal of a late-stage trial in patients with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, a progressive condition that causes irreversible lung scarring.

The trial evaluated two doses of admilparant against a primary goal of improving lung function at 52 weeks. A 60-milligram dose, taken twice daily, demonstrated a statistically significant benefit over placebo in preserving lung function, whereas a 120-milligram dose didn't achieve statistical significance.

The results show a lack of dose response, with higher doses failing to produce a stronger effect. RBC Capital Markets analyst Trung Huynh called the outcome "confounding," saying it "requires further explanation."
Leerink Partners analyst David Risinger expressed similar skepticism.
"We await detailed results to better understand the drug's efficacy," he wrote, though he noted the data could still support regulatory approval.
Shares of Contineum Therapeutics, which is developing a rival treatment, cratered 30% on Monday. The much-smaller drugmaker has a market capitalization of just $503 million.

Views elsewhere on Wall Street were more positive. William Blair's Matt Phipps noted that while questions remain around admilparant's magnitude of benefit, the lower-dose data alone "is likely to open a blockbuster opportunity."

Both readouts come amid the drugmaker's search for its next big revenue driver. Bristol Myers faces a major patent cliff in 2028, when key protections begin to expire for blockbuster drugs Opdivo and Eliquis. The latter is co-commercialized with Pfizer.

In turn, Bristol Myers is leaning on newer drugs to replace lost revenue. Chief among that effort is antipsychotic medication Cobenfy, still viewed as a blockbuster hopeful despite a slower-than-expected commercial start and a string of clinical setbacks.
